title: Theo Cashed Out $30K. It Cost Him $228K 😬
description:
Nora and Theo both change jobs at 35, each with the same $30K in a 401(k). Nora rolls hers straight into her new plan. Theo cashes out, loses $9,600 to the penalty and income tax, and buys a jet ski with the $20,400 left. Thirty years later, Nora's pile is about $228K. The jet ski is at the bottom of the lake.

Leaving a job doesn't have to mean touching the money: a direct rollover isn't taxed now.

Would you cash out, or leave it alone? Tell me why 👇

Follow for more numbers that change how you spend.

⚠️ Fictional characters, illustration only. Assumes age 35 to 65, 7% a year (not guaranteed), no new deposits, before tax at withdrawal. Theo: 10% IRS early-withdrawal additional tax plus the 22% federal bracket on the whole $30K; state tax would be extra, and some penalty exceptions exist. Sources: IRS "Exceptions to tax on early distributions", IRS Topic 413 (rollovers), Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 brackets). This is not financial advice.
